title: Test Your Understanding: Leader Election and Distributed Locks
description: Split-brain, TTL locks, fencing tokens, and when to use coordination services — not just definitions.

questions.question: Why do horizontally scaled apps need leader election or distributed locks for certain jobs?

options.text: To increase HTTP throughput on every node
To ensure cluster-wide singleton work (cron, migrations) runs at most once at a time
To replace load balancers
To guarantee exactly-once message delivery from a queue

questions.explanation: Stateless request handling scales out naturally. Background jobs, coordinators, and exclusive resources need coordination so multiple nodes don't all assume they're responsible.

questions.question: What is split-brain in a distributed cluster?

options.text: When all nodes agree on a single leader
When two or more nodes both believe they are leader or hold the same exclusive role
When the cluster has zero leaders forever
When clients use sticky sessions

questions.explanation: Split-brain means coordination failed — two sides both act as leader. That leads to duplicate cron runs, conflicting writes, or inconsistent cluster state.

questions.question: Why do TTL-based distributed locks include an expiration time?

options.text: To improve cache hit rate
So a crashed lock holder cannot block the resource forever
To encrypt lock values
To guarantee linearizable reads

questions.explanation: If a process dies without releasing a lock, TTL lets another process eventually acquire it. The trade-off is a slow holder may outlive its TTL unless renewal and fencing are handled.

questions.question: What problem do fencing tokens solve?

options.text: Slow DNS lookups
Stale lock holders writing after their lease expired — storage rejects lower tokens
Hot keys on a hash ring
CDN cache poisoning

questions.explanation: After TTL expiry, a delayed process may still try to write. Fencing tokens monotonically increase with each lock acquisition; the resource rejects writes with outdated tokens.

questions.question: When is etcd or ZooKeeper a better fit than a naive Redis SET NX lock?

options.text: Never — Redis always suffices
When you need consensus-backed coordination, watches, and stronger election semantics
Only for static asset caching
When you want every node to run the cron job

questions.explanation: Coordination services are built for quorum, linearizable lock paths, and session/ephemeral nodes. Redis locks can work for simpler cases but have well-known edge cases under partitions and long pauses.

questions.question: You run the same `@Scheduled` cron on every instance in a three-pod deployment with no lock. What happens?

options.text: The job runs once — the JVM coordinates automatically
The job can run up to three times per schedule — once per pod
Only the pod with the lowest IP runs the job
Kubernetes blocks duplicate cron automatically

questions.explanation: Each pod is independent unless you add leader election, a distributed lock, or move scheduling to a single external trigger. Three pods often means triple execution.

questions.question: Why should lock release compare the holder's token before deleting the key?

options.text: To compress lock metadata
To prevent one process from deleting another process's lock after TTL expiry and re-acquisition
To enable CDN caching
To speed up leader election

questions.explanation: If A's lock expired and B acquired the lock, A must not delete B's key on cleanup. Compare-and-delete (owner token matches) avoids accidentally releasing someone else's lock.

questions.question: Making background jobs idempotent removes the need for leader election or locks entirely.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Idempotency limits damage when coordination fails or duplicates occur — it's essential but not always enough (API rate limits, user-visible duplicate emails, conflicting writes). Coordination and idempotency work together.
